content:
A sending church can love you and still be wrong to send you this year. Formal assessment exists so people who have watched other planters can say what they see, before a network puts its name, money, and people behind a new church.

This guide teaches the sequence many sending networks use. You complete an assessment. You receive feedback. You work a development plan. Then the leaders who would send or support you decide. The assessor does not own that decision. Everyfield does not either.

---

## The sequence many networks use

Before many networks agree to send you, or to support the plant, they want three things in order.

1. An assessment. Trained assessors watch how you teach, relate, and handle pressure. If you are married, your spouse is usually in the room with you.
2. Written feedback. You hear strengths, concerns, and what still needs work.
3. A development plan. You and your sending leaders name what you will do with that feedback before they treat you as ready to send.

A weekend of interviews is not the whole pathway. The decision belongs to the people who would actually send you.

Centers do not all run the same week. Some gather you for several days. Some start with forms, a first conversation, and questions sent to people who know you, then invite you to interviews. Ask your sending church which steps they require. Another network's packet is not yours.

<Callout type="important">
Everyfield does not score your calling, certify you as a planter, or stop you from creating a plant. An outside assessment is separate from opening a plant in the app. A missing result is not a lock.
</Callout>

---

## Who decides

Assessors watch and write. Sending leaders decide.

The church or network that would sponsor you chooses whether to send you and whether to support the work. A center can recommend you and still not place you. A center can raise concerns and still leave the final word with the leaders who know your life. Treat the written recommendation as counsel with weight. It does not replace your church.

Outside affirmation matters. It is not the last word on calling. If your sending church will not affirm you, take that seriously. They may see what you cannot. Their no is not the same thing as God closing the call forever. Their yes is not a substitute for your own obedience.

<Callout type="scripture">
*"Then, when they had fasted and prayed and laid their hands on them, they sent them away."* — Acts 13:3 (LSB)
</Callout>

In Acts, the church in Antioch sent. Copy that pattern, not a software score. Leaders pray, name the work, and take responsibility for the sending. Everyfield will not make that call. The app does not judge character, fitness, or spiritual health, and it does not gate plant creation on an assessment result.

---

## How to prepare

Start before anyone hands you a packet.

Write a plain account of your ministry. Where have you led people to faith? Where have you quit? Where does your household already feel the cost?

If you are married, talk with your spouse before you talk with assessors. Ask what they are willing to carry, what they fear, and what they will not pretend to support. A spouse who is surprised in the interview means you skipped the harder conversation at home. If you are single, name the people who will tell you the truth about pace, loneliness, and money.

Give references who have seen you lead, not only people who like you. Some processes send questions to people you name, so your self-portrait can be compared with theirs. Ask them to be specific. "Hard worker" helps less than a sentence about a commitment you missed and how you repaired it.

- [ ] Write where you have borne fruit, where you have failed, and what you are still hiding
- [ ] Talk with your spouse, or with the family this plant would uproot, and write what they actually said
- [ ] Ask your sending pastor what this network requires before it will send or support a planter
- [ ] Choose references who have seen you under pressure, and ask them to be specific
- [ ] Read the packet and list who receives the report, how long they keep it, and what a not yet means there

<Callout type="tip">
Ask who will read the report and whether you may share it with your coach. You want feedback you can use with the people responsible for you.
</Callout>

---

## What the days look like

Expect to be watched, not only interviewed.

A typical center mixes personal interviews with work you do in front of people. You may preach, or play a recording of a sermon. You may work a case, sit in a small group, or sketch how you would start a church. Assessors are looking for patterns.

If you are married, plan on your spouse being part of the conversation. Questions often cover conflict, money, pace, and who carries the hidden work at home. Answer from the life you actually live.

Do not expect a settled answer in the hallway. The people who assessed you may need hours, or longer, to compare notes before they speak. Wait for the written word. A kind goodbye is not a yes.

---

## What the feedback should tell you

Useful feedback names what the assessors saw. It is not a color, and it is not a rank you can post.

You should leave with strengths, concerns, and what still has to change. Some centers also name a recommendation. Full approval. Approval with conditions, such as more training or a clearer fit of place. A wait before they will look again. Or a recommendation not to begin a new church. Those words are about readiness for this send. They do not settle your calling.

Read the report with your spouse if you have one, then with your sending pastor and your coach. Ask what they saw that you have avoided. Ask what would have to be true before this network would send you. Put a date on the next piece of work.

If the report is only praise, ask for the concerns. If it is only criticism, ask what is already strong. You cannot build a plan on a blank page. The useful report becomes training and supervision, not a souvenir.

---

## When the answer is not yet

A not yet is a decision about timing and preparation. Treat it that way.

Some centers will not reconsider you until a stated waiting period has passed. Others leave the timing to your sending church. Do not collect assessments until one of them says yes. That wastes the people who told you the truth, and it teaches you to shop for a softer room.

Ask your sending leaders what would change their answer. Write that as a plan you can finish. More fruit in evangelism. A repaired conflict. A year under a Senior Pastor who will watch your work. A family decision that is no longer vague. Then do the work where you are. Keep serving while you discern. Preparation during a wait is the obedience in front of you, not a pause in it.

You can ask again after that work is visible. Bring the same report, plus evidence, not a new speech. If the leaders still say no, believe they mean it for this send. Do not use Everyfield, or a second weekend, to get around the people responsible for you.

<Callout type="warning">
Do not hide a not yet from your sending church. The leaders who would send you need the same report you hold. A quiet second application is not preparation.
</Callout>

---

## Take it back to your leaders

The assessment is finished when the conversation with your sending leaders is finished, not when you leave the center.

Walk the report with the people who would send or support you. Agree on the plan, or agree that they will not send you yet. If you have a coach, give that person the same pages. A coach can help you work the plan. A coach does not replace the church that would pray, name the work, and send you.

Then stay in ordinary work. Pray. Serve. Tell the truth at home. The goal is a life your church can affirm without squinting, not a cleaner application.

---

## Mistakes that waste the process

| Mistake | What it costs |
| --- | --- |
| Treating the assessor as the one who calls you | You skip the church that has to live with the send |
| Hiding strain at home | The feedback cannot protect the people who would pay the cost |
| Asking references to sell you | The report describes a person your leaders will not recognize |
| Shopping centers for a yes | You learn to outrun counsel instead of using it |
| Waiting for an app to clear you | No software here certifies calling or blocks a plant |

If your network has no formal center, do not invent one, and do not stall. Ask your sending pastor for the same three moves in a simpler form. An honest review. Candid feedback from people who know you. A written plan before they agree to send or support you. The pathway is that sequence, not a brand of weekend.

claim_check.notes: Owner review by Sebastian; no model review per his 2026-10-26 instruction.

rulings: Bryan ruled B11 = Option B: "Formal network pathway" (2026-10-26).

Wording call: teach the sequence as the pathway many sending networks use, not as an Everyfield requirement. Everyfield does not certify calling or block plant creation (REQ-EVR-001, REQ-PI-018, REQ-PI-046). Assessment remains one outside affirmation, consistent with discovery/is-church-planting-your-calling, not the final word on calling.

Wording call: do not name assessment providers, networks, or Ridley's 13 characteristics in the body. The fetched Ridley attribution was a network restatement, not Ridley's own publication, and naming one model would read as an endorsement. Describe competencies only in general terms.

Wording call: do not state a universal waiting period, fee, date, or location. Some centers name a waiting period before reconsideration. The reader should ask their own sending leaders what would reopen the question.
Wording call: gender-neutral wording where source pages say wife, husband, or candidate couple. Spouse and family language covers married and single readers.
